task.title: Document language
task.shortdesc: The language of the text decides how CSSMedia hyphenates words, which quotation marks it uses, how it changes letter case and which elements the :lang() selector matches. CSSMedia reads the language from the xml:lang attribute. If your XML names the language in another attribute, use the CSSMedia -cssmedia-lang property to say which one.

context.p: A language tag is a short code that names a language, such as en for English, fr for French or zh-Hans for Chinese in simplified characters. The xml:lang attribute is defined by the XML specification. It holds a language tag and applies to the element that carries it and to everything inside that element.

XML can use any element and attribute names, so CSSMedia cannot know which other attribute holds a language. A vocabulary such as DocBook 4 uses a plain lang attribute. Names such as para and lang below are examples. Replace them with names used in your XML.

info.p: When your XML already has xml:lang attributes, you do not write anything in the stylesheet. An element has the language of the nearest xml:lang on itself or on an ancestor.

stepxmp.pre: <article xml:lang="en"> <para>This paragraph is in English.</para> <para xml:lang="fr">Ce paragraphe est en français.</para> </article>

step.cmd: Take the language from another attribute

info.p: The -cssmedia-lang property is a CSSMedia extension. It is not a standard CSS property, so its name has the vendor prefix -cssmedia-. It sets the language of the elements it is applied to.

row.entry: The property does not set the language of the element. This is the initial value.
A language tag written between quotation marks, such as "fr". An empty string is the same as none.

info.p: The property is not inherited, but the language it sets reaches the content of the element, as xml:lang does. Use attr() to read the language from an attribute:

stepxmp.pre: <book lang="en"> <para>This paragraph is in English.</para> <para lang="de">Dieser Absatz ist auf Deutsch.</para> </book>

info.p: * selects every element. attr(lang) reads the value of the lang attribute of each element. The first para has no lang attribute, so attr() supplies an empty string and the paragraph keeps the language of book. The second para is in German.
You can also write the language in the stylesheet:
For each element, CSSMedia takes the first of these that exists:

ol.li: The language set by -cssmedia-lang on the element.
The xml:lang attribute of the element itself.
The language of its parent element.

info.p: An element with both a lang attribute that your rule reads and an xml:lang attribute takes the language from lang.

A rule that sets -cssmedia-lang cannot depend on the language. A selector such as :lang(fr) or :dir(rtl) never matches while CSSMedia decides the language, so those selectors have no effect on the -cssmedia-lang declarations. They work as usual on all other properties, and they see the language that -cssmedia-lang gave.
